lesson.title: Writing the Recommendation No One Can Wave Away
lesson.summary: This chapter teaches how to turn a completed evaluation into a written recommendation that states its conclusion up front, traces every claim back to real evidence, and gives a decision-maker something concrete to approve or reject.
lesson.body:
Everything the decision framework and evidence-based evaluation chapters taught you produces, at the end, a pile of evidence: scored criteria, pilot metrics, cost estimates, risk notes. None of that evidence changes anything by itself. It has to become a document someone with authority to spend money or say no actually reads, understands in one pass, and can act on. That document is the recommendation, and writing one badly is one of the most common ways a genuinely good technical evaluation dies before it does any good.

The single most important rule is to state the recommendation first, not last. Technical writers trained on lab reports instinctively build up to a conclusion: background, method, findings, and only then, on the last page, the actual recommendation. Decision-makers read the opposite way. They want the answer in the first sentence, then the evidence in case they want to check your reasoning or defend the decision to someone else later. We recommend piloting a permissioned ledger for cold-chain temperature logging with the three named retail partners, budget capped at the pilot stage, decision point in four months, belongs in sentence one, not paragraph twelve.

The second rule is that the evidence has to be traceable back to the decision framework and evidence-based evaluation work, not restated as new claims. If the recommendation says the carrier's current process has an unacceptable gap rate, that number should trace directly to the pilot metrics you actually measured, not to a vendor's marketing deck or an executive's hunch. This is where evidence-based evaluation pays off directly: a recommendation built on traceable, sourced evidence survives hostile questioning, and a recommendation built on vibes does not, no matter how well written the prose is.

The third rule, and the one people skip most often because it feels like weakening their own case, is to name the alternatives you considered and say honestly why you rejected them. A recommendation that only argues for its own conclusion looks like advocacy, and experienced decision-makers discount advocacy on sight. A recommendation that says we also considered a shared database run by a neutral third-party auditor, and rejected it because no candidate auditor had the food-safety domain trust required by all four parties, shows the reader you ran the actual decision flowchart rather than deciding in advance and reasoning backward. This is also the place to be explicit about what would change your mind, since a recommendation with no stated conditions for reversal reads as either overconfident or untested.

Fourth, state the risks and the caveats plainly rather than burying them in a risk appendix nobody reads. If the pilot succeeded on one supply route but you have real uncertainty about whether it generalizes to the carrier's other regions, say so in the recommendation itself, in a sentence, not three sections away. Decision-makers who discover a hidden caveat after approving something stop trusting the next recommendation from you, which costs you more credibility than the caveat itself would have.

Finally, end with a concrete, boundaried next step, not an open-ended one. Approve a four-month pilot, budget capped at the amount specified in the attached cost estimate, with a go or no-go decision at the review date, is something an executive can approve in a meeting. We should explore blockchain further is not a decision anyone can make, which means it will sit unapproved and unrejected indefinitely, the worst possible outcome for the time you spent building the evidence.

Put it together for Meridian Foods. The recommendation memo opens: we recommend a four-month pilot of a permissioned blockchain network for cold-chain temperature logging, limited to one grower, the primary carrier, and one retail partner, with success measured against two fixed metrics tied to reading capture completeness and dispute resolution. The evidence section that follows doesn't repeat that claim, it supports it: the current paper-and-spreadsheet process has produced disputes that took weeks to resolve during past recall investigations, evidence pulled directly from the decision framework's cost-of-status-quo analysis. The alternatives section explains why a shared database run by a neutral auditor was considered and rejected, tracing straight back to gate three of the decision flowchart. The risk section flags the connectivity gap in rural pickup zones honestly, before anyone else can raise it as a gotcha. And it closes with a specific ask: approve the pilot budget, set the four-month review date, nothing vaguer than that.

A recommendation like that can be wrong and still be well written, because being wrong in a traceable, falsifiable way is recoverable. A vague recommendation that never quite says what should happen next is the one that wastes everyone's evidence-gathering effort, whether it turns out right or wrong.
